summary: Elevates RFC 7344 to the Standards Track and adds a method for initial DNSSEC trust setup and for removing a secure entry point, so a parent zone can manage a child's DS records.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC lets a child DNS zone signal that its parent should change the delegation's DNSSEC records. It adds procedures for starting DNSSEC and for asking the parent to remove the DS records.

questions: what are cds and cdnskey records
how to remove a ds record
subtitle: Lets a child DNS zone ask its parent to add, update or remove DS records using CDS or CDNSKEY.

tldr.problem: RFC 7344 covered key rollover but did not define initial trust setup or a signal for removing all DS records.
tldr.mechanism: A child publishes CDS or CDNSKEY records, and the parent applies its acceptance policy. A fixed delete record asks the parent to remove the DS set.
tldr.outcome: The RFC adds initial trust and deletion procedures and promotes RFC 7344 to the Standards Track. RFC 9615 later updates it.

today: RFC 8078 is a Proposed Standard, updates RFC 7344 and is updated by RFC 9615.

sections.title: What CDS and CDNSKEY Add
sections.content:
CDS and CDNSKEY records let a child zone signal changes to its secure entry point at the parent. RFC 7344 described key rollover, but did not define initial trust setup or a signal to remove DNSSEC from the delegation.

This document adds those two operations and promotes RFC 7344 from Informational to the Standards Track. In this RFC, CDS refers to either a CDS or CDNSKEY record.
sections.plainLanguage: The child zone can publish a request for changes to the parent's DS records. This RFC adds requests for first-time setup and for removing DNSSEC.

sections.title: Three Operations for DS Records
sections.content:
A child may ask its parent to publish an initial DS record set, update the set during a key rollover, or remove all DS records to turn off DNSSEC validation. Key rollover is defined in RFC 7344; this document defines initial setup and removal.

Publishing CDS or CDNSKEY signals that the child wants the corresponding parent DS records synchronized. Each parent or parental agent should have an acceptance policy for each operation.
sections.plainLanguage: The three operations are to start DNSSEC, change keys while keeping trust, or remove the DS records. The parent decides whether a request meets its acceptance policy.

sections.title: Parent Policies for Initial Trust
sections.content:
The parent can accept a request through an authenticated channel, apply extra checks, wait and monitor the child records, issue a challenge that proves control of the zone, or publish DS together with NS for a new child delegation.

The policies have different security properties. For checks and challenges, the RFC recommends monitoring the child from varied network locations. The details of how a third-party DNS operator submits its information are outside the RFC's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A parent can authenticate the request, perform extra checks, wait, ask for proof in the child zone, or publish DS when creating a new delegation. The RFC describes these as possible acceptance policies.

sections.title: The DNSSEC Delete Record
sections.content:
Algorithm number zero signals that the parent should remove the entire DS record set. A delete request must contain exactly one record in one of these forms: CDS 0 0 0 0 or CDNSKEY 0 3 0 0. The record is signed like a regular CDS or CDNSKEY record.

After validating the request and applying its acceptance checks, the parent must remove the DS records. The child waits for a sufficient time based on parental TTLs before turning off DNSSEC.
sections.plainLanguage: The delete request has one exact form made of zero values. The parent removes the DS set only after it verifies that record and accepts the request.

sections.title: Security and IANA Assignment
sections.content:
Removing DNSSEC reduces a domain's security, so the RFC says to consider it only after other options. A parent should check that an initial CDS or CDNSKEY set is visible from diverse locations and that the zone will validate correctly after publishing DS.

IANA assigned algorithm number 0 the meaning “Delete DS” and mnemonic DELETE. In DNSKEY and DS records, a validator treats algorithm zero as unknown rather than as a valid signature algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: Turning off DNSSEC reduces protection and should be done carefully. Before enabling it, the parent should check that the published request is visible and the zone validates.

viz.caption: THE TWO VALID DELETE RECORD FORMS

items.title: Authenticated channel
items.text: Parent retrieves the child's record after an authenticated notice.

items.title: Extra checks
items.text: Parent verifies the requester or asks for confirmation.

items.title: Delay
items.text: Parent monitors the child record over time.

items.title: Challenge
items.text: Requester proves control by publishing a record in the child zone.

items.title: From inception
items.text: Parent publishes DS with NS for a new delegation.
